course_profile.one_sentence_summary: A foundational course covering essential discrete mathematics concepts, including set theory, graph theory, mathematical logic, and automata theory, tailored for software engineering students.
course_profile.short_summary: This course introduces students to the mathematical foundations of computer science. It covers sets, relations, algebraic structures, Boolean algebra, propositional and predicate logic, graph theory, and finite automata, focusing on formalizing, analyzing, and transforming mathematical models for software development.

source_coverage.coverage_comment: Information extracted from a comprehensive official syllabus document (working program) for the course.

evidence: The syllabus explicitly states there are no prerequisites and the discipline is foundational, implying only standard high-school graduation level math is needed.
Section 1 covers set theory, set operations, and algebra of sets, practiced in Practice session 1.
Lectures 5-8 and practical sessions 6-10 deeply cover Boolean algebra, normal forms, and multiple methods for minimizing Boolean functions.
Section 5 focuses on mathematical logic, including deductive conclusions, quantifiers, and normal forms.

raw_mentions: Найкоротші відстані та шляхи у мережах
evidence: Section 6 thoroughly covers graph theory, including trees, shortest path algorithms (Dijkstra, Ford-Bellman), and network flows.
Section 7 introduces automata theory, including FSMs, Moore and Mealy machines, and their minimization.
The final parts of Section 7 cover algebraic operations with languages, Chomsky normal forms, and context-free languages.

theoretical_understanding: Understand the basic concepts of discrete mathematics, including sets, relations, algebraic structures, and boolean algebra.
Comprehend the principles of propositional and predicate logic.
Understand the properties of graphs, trees, and finite automata.
Recognize the hierarchy of formal grammars and languages.
practical_implementation: Perform operations on sets and relations.
Minimize boolean functions using various algorithmic methods (Karnaugh maps, Quine-McCluskey, etc.).
Apply graph algorithms to find shortest paths, spanning trees, and maximum network flows.
Construct and minimize Moore and Mealy state machines.
analysis_validation: Analyze mathematical models to evaluate their complexity.
Evaluate the equivalence of boolean formulas and formal grammar normal forms.
architecture_design: Formalize abstract mathematical problems into appropriate discrete models (graphs, automata) suitable for software engineering tasks.

expected_artifacts: Written solutions for boolean minimization problems
Graph models and step-by-step algorithm execution traces
Constructed logic and state machine diagrams
implementation_tasks: Applying graph traversal and optimization algorithms by hand
Converting truth tables to minimal boolean expressions
engineering_practices: Formal definition of requirements into discrete mathematical structures

curricular_relations.reason: Concepts of sets and algebra of sets form the foundation for understanding Boolean algebra.
Set operations are heavily analogous and structurally foundational to logical operations.
Logic principles are essential for defining state transitions and automata behaviors.
State machines are commonly visualized and analyzed as directed graphs.

what_student_can_understand: The fundamental discrete mathematical structures underlying computer science.
The principles of formal logic and how they apply to software correctness.
How different classes of formal languages are recognized by computational automata.
what_student_can_build: Formal models using sets, relations, and graphs.
State transition diagrams for deterministic and non-deterministic systems.
what_student_can_apply: Graph algorithms for practical routing and network flow problems.

evidence.claim: The course has no prerequisites and is foundational.
The course covers detailed boolean function minimization techniques.
